{"id": "2:286/q28", "question": "How do pardon, forgiveness, and mercy differ?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q28/p1", "position": "Pardon erases punishment, while forgiveness conceals sins.", "reasons": "JISHUMI: One interpretation asks God to erase sins and cover them. forgiveness means concealing faults so the believer is not exposed before people."}, {"id": "2:286/q28/p20", "position": "Pardon and forgiveness precede the request for mercy because clearing away faults comes before adorning the servant with favor.", "reasons": "BURSEVI: Pardon and forgiveness precede the request for mercy because clearing away faults comes before adorning the servant with favor."}, {"id": "2:286/q28/p21", "position": "An alternative assigns pardon to deeds, forgiveness to words, and mercy to the weighing of the scales.", "reasons": "ALUSI-FULL reporting قيل: An alternative assigns pardon to deeds, forgiveness to words, and mercy to the weighing of the scales."}, {"id": "2:286/q28/p22", "position": "Alternatively, pardon, forgiveness, and mercy generalize the preceding specific requests and are their foundations, making this one encompassing prayer.", "reasons": "IBNASHUR-FULL: Alternatively, pardon, forgiveness, and mercy generalize the preceding specific requests and are their foundations, making this one encompassing prayer."}, {"id": "2:286/q28/p23", "position": "The three pleas progress from specific effect to general source: pardon removes sin's effect or recorded punishment, forgiveness removes and veils its inward state, and mercy is God's gift covering both.", "reasons": "TABATABAI: The three pleas progress from specific effect to general source: pardon removes sin's effect or recorded punishment, forgiveness removes and veils its inward state, and mercy is God's gift covering both."}, {"id": "2:286/q28/p24", "position": "Pardon, forgiveness, and mercy seek relief from sins.", "reasons": "MUQATIL: Pardon, forgiveness, and mercy seek relief from sins."}]}
{"id": "2:286/q29", "question": "What does مَوْلَىٰنَا mean?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q29/p1", "position": "Mawlā means guardian, protector, helper, or manager of affairs.", "reasons": "IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB: Mawlānā means our guardian or protector. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas and the exegetes explain Mawlana as our helper or protector, as in the verses calling God the believers' wali or mawla. WAHIDI-BASIT: Anyone joined to you and protected by your strength is your mawla; this explains calling paternal kin mawali, while poetry distinguishes allied clients from relatives and mawla can mean a guardian of one's affairs. JISHUMI: Mawlā here means our guardian and protector, the one with greatest claim over us. BAGHAWI-FULL: God is their helper, protector, and patron. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Calling God our mawla praises Him, draws the supplicant near, and thanks Him; mawla derives from wali and denotes guardianship. TABRISI: Mawlānā means our protector, the one entitled to direct our affairs, and our helper. IBNJAWZI-ZAD: Anta mawlānā means “You are our protector.” RAZI-FULL: Here Mawla means helper or protector, as in 8:40, 2:257, 66:4, and 47:11. QURTUBI-FULL: Mawlana means our protector and guard
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<chunk 92, part 1 of 0..5>>
ian. QURTUBI-FULL: Mawlana means our protector and helper. SAMIN-DURR: The fāʾ marks causation: because God is their protector and manages their affairs, they ask Him to grant victory over their enemies. IBNKATHIR-FULL: Mawlana means our protector and helper; believers trust and rely on God, with no power or strength except through Him. BIQAI-FULL: Biqāʿī explains mawlā as the enduring guardian who maintains care for those who entrust Him with what they cannot accomplish themselves. BIQAI-FULL: Mawlā also means the one who brings guardianship to fruition through closeness and turning toward the ward; the petition seeks bodily reward in paradise and spiritual delight in vision. BURSEVI: The plea asks God to help against disbelievers and repel their harm, as a guardian should defend those in his care; victory may come through conquest, argument, or defense. ALUSI-FULL: When mawlā and sayyid are both used, Arabic usage puts mawlā first; al-Khansāʾ's verse is cited as evidence, though Al-Alusi has reservations about the criticism of the reverse order. ALUSI-FULL: The clause may be understood as an instruction to say: You are our patron. ALUSI-FULL: The fāʾ signals causation: because God is their patron and manager, they ask Him to grant victory, like asking generosity from a generous person. IBNASHUR-FULL: The appeal to God's patronage rests on a patron's duty to treat dependents gently. IBNASHUR-FULL: The فاء derives the plea for victory from God's role as patron, since a patron is expected to aid those under his care. IBNASHUR-FULL: The request's derivation from God's established guardianship over believers strengthens its insistence and recalls 2:257. TABATABAI: Mawlā means a supporter who takes charge of the supported person's affairs, not just any helper; God is believers' guardian and protector. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting يونس: Yunus explains the Prophet's saying Whoever has me as his mawla, Ali is his mawla to mean whoever has me as his wali. WAHIDI-BASIT: The report calling Muzayna, Juhayna, Aslam, and Ghifar God's and His Messenger's mawali means they are His allies; Al-Ajjaj's verse likewise uses mawali for allies of truth."}, {"id": "2:286/q29/p2", "position": "Mawlā means master or owner.", "reasons": "THALABI: Calling God our master means asking Him as helper, protector, guardian, and patron to grant victory over the disbelievers. MAWARDI-FULL: Mawlana means either our master and owner or our protector and helper. KASHSHAF-FULL: “Our mawlā” may mean our master, since we are His servants; our helper; or the one who manages our affairs. KASHSHAF-FULL: They ask for victory because a master should aid his servants, because this is God’s customary way, or because managing their affairs is His concern. RAZI-FULL: Calling God their Mawla expresses utmost humility and dependence: God gives every blessing and honor, as a guardian tends a child or a master orders a servant’s affairs. BAYDAWI-FULL: Mawlā here means our master. BAYDAWI-FULL: The plea follows from a master’s duty to aid his clients against enemies; alternatively, “the unbelieving people” means unbelievers generally. NASAFI-FULL: Mawlā can mean our master, helper, or the one who manages our affairs. NASAFI-FULL: The request for victory follows because a master is expected to aid his servants. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Mawla derives from waliya and can function as a verbal, temporal, or locative noun; in the sense of ruler, master, helper, or kinsman it is a lexicalized noun. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The ف in فانصرنا signals causation: because God is their master and manager, they ask Him to help them against enemies and instill courage while weakening the enemy. BURSEVI: Mawlānā can mean our master while we are His servants, our helper, or the one who manages our affairs. ALUSI-FULL: Mawlānā means our owner and master, or the one who manages our affairs; it is a verbal noun used for an agent. ELMALILI: Mawlana means our patron, owner and master, guardian of our affairs, and helper; Elmalılı links it to the declaration that God is the protector of those who believe."}]}

{"id": "2:286/q33", "question": "How are the petition verbs inflected?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q33/p1", "position": "The Basrans treat waʿfu as an imperative in form but indeclinable; the Kūfans make it jussive, as with the following requests.", "reasons": "NAHHAS reporting البصريون: The Basrans treat waʿfu as an imperative in form but indeclinable; the Kūfans make it jussive, as with the following requests."}, {"id": "2:286/q33/p2", "position": "Some call prohibitive la a request particle so the label includes supplication as well as prohibition; here la is a prayer asking God not to hold the speakers accountable.", "reasons": "BURHAN reporting بعضهم: Some call prohibitive la a request particle so the label includes supplication as well as prohibition; here la is a prayer asking God not to hold the speakers accountable."}, {"id": "2:286/q33/p3", "position": "Prohibitive lā is used with a present verb, makes it jussive, and places the action in the future; it may express either prohibition or supplication.", "reasons": "ITQAN: Prohibitive lā is used with a present verb, makes it jussive, and places the action in the future; it may express either prohibition or supplication."}, {"id": "2:286/q33/p4", "position": "Ibn Asfur gives inconsistent accounts, alternately saying the governing verb may be stated or must remain implicit.", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting ابن عصفور: Ibn Asfur gives inconsistent accounts, alternately saying the governing verb may be stated or must remain implicit."}, {"id": "2:286/q33/p5", "position": "The coordinating and answer uses of lā do not occur in the Qur’an.", "reasons": "ITQAN: The coordinating and answer uses of lā do not occur in the Qur’an."}]}
{"id": "2:286/q34", "question": "Did 2:286 abrogate the accounting of 2:284?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q34/p1", "position": "2:286 lifted or abrogated the earlier accounting for unacted thoughts.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: Some interpreters say that the earlier ruling about inward thoughts was abrogated by 2:286; Abu Hurayra reports people’s distress and God affirming their concluding petitions. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbas explains that Ibn ʿUmar feared people would perish under 2:284; 2:286 then abrogated accountability for inner whisperings while retaining accountability for speech and deeds. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas said Ibn Umar wept over 2:284 as the Companions had, and that 2:286 abrogated it. TAB-FULL reporting سعيد بن جبير: Saʿid ibn Jubayr reported that 2:286 abrogated the earlier statement that God would account for what people disclosed or concealed. TAB-FULL reporting عامر: Amir said the verse about hidden thoughts being accounted for was abrogated by the following verse, 2:286. TAB-FULL reporting الشعبي: Al-Shaʿbi said 2:286 abrogated 2:284, which had said that God accounts for what people disclose or hide. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbas says 2:284 greatly distressed the Companions, who were told to say “we hear and obey”; it was abrogated through 2:285–286, excusing inner thoughts while holding them to actions. TAB-FULL reporting الشعبي: Al-Shaʿbi reported that the burden of 2:284 lasted until 2:286 came, whereupon the latter abrogated what preceded it. TAB-FULL reporting ابن مسعود: Ibn Masʿud said accountability for hidden thoughts preceded 2:286, which abrogated the earlier verse. TAB-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujahid and his co-transmitters reported that 2:286 abrogated the earlier verse about disclosed or concealed thoughts. TAB-FULL reporting عكرمة، وعامر: Ikrima and Amir reported the same position: 2:286 abrogated the earlier accounting for hidden thoughts. TAB-FULL reporting الحسن: Al-Hasan said 2:286 erased 2:284, including its statement about what is disclosed or hidden.
